title: Russian Doll Envelopes
description: Brute force to optimized: O(n squared) pairwise nesting DP versus reducing to the Longest Increasing Subsequence problem via a careful sort.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a 2D array envelopes where envelopes[i] = [width, height], one envelope can fit inside another if and only if both its width and height are strictly smaller than the other's. Return the maximum number of envelopes that can be nested inside each other (like Russian dolls), forming one chain.

blocks.text: A valid nesting chain requires both width and height to strictly increase from one envelope to the next in the chain. This is a 2D version of finding the longest increasing subsequence, and the key trick is reducing it to a 1D problem by sorting first.

blocks.title: Analogy: Stacking Russian Nesting Dolls by Two Measurements
blocks.text: Picture a set of nesting dolls, each with a width and a height, where one doll fits inside another only if it is strictly smaller in EVERY dimension. Sorting them by width first (with a careful tie-breaking rule for same-width dolls) reduces the puzzle to finding the longest run of strictly increasing heights among them.

blocks.caption: Sorting by width ascending (ties broken by height descending) reduces nesting to Longest Increasing Subsequence on heights

blocks.text: Result: 3. The longest chain is [2,3] -> [5,4] -> [6,7], nesting 3 envelopes.

Before considering this a full 2D problem, notice that sorting by width first FIXES the width ordering, so only the height dimension needs to strictly increase along a valid chain, which reduces directly to the well-known Longest Increasing Subsequence problem, but the tie-breaking rule for equal widths needs care.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If envelopes are sorted by width ascending, any chain that also has strictly increasing heights (in this sorted order) automatically has strictly increasing widths too, EXCEPT when two envelopes share the same width, which must never be allowed in a chain.

Observation 2: To prevent same-width envelopes from being treated as a valid consecutive pair in the height-based subsequence, sort ties (equal widths) by height in DESCENDING order; this way, among same-width envelopes, only one can ever be picked into an increasing height subsequence at a time, since their heights appear in decreasing order and cannot form an increasing pair with each other.

Observation 3: After this careful sort, the problem exactly becomes finding the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) of the height values.

Observation 4: LIS itself can be solved in O(n log n) using a "patience sorting" technique: maintain a list of the smallest possible tail values for increasing subsequences of each length, using binary search to find where each new height belongs.

This leads to sorting envelopes by width ascending (ties by height descending), then computing the Longest Increasing Subsequence of the resulting height sequence using the O(n log n) patience-sorting technique.
Use O(n squared) dynamic programming directly on pairs: for each envelope, find the best chain ending there by checking all earlier envelopes that could nest inside it.

items: Sort envelopes by width ascending (ties broken by height ascending is fine here since we check both dimensions directly in the DP).
For each envelope i, compute dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all j before i where envelopes[j] fits strictly inside envelopes[i] in both dimensions.
The answer is the maximum value in dp.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking both dimensions directly for every pair is the most literal implementation of the nesting condition.
This costs O(n squared), too slow for n up to 10^5.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking all pairs.
Space: O(n) for the dp array.
Limitation: the 2D nesting condition can be reduced to a 1D Longest Increasing Subsequence problem via a careful sort, solvable in O(n log n) instead of O(n squared).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking both dimensions directly is unnecessary after sorting: sorting by width ascending already guarantees width strictly increases along any subsequence that skips equal-width groups correctly, so only the height dimension needs an increasing-subsequence check.

The critical tie-breaking trick: sorting SAME-WIDTH envelopes by height DESCENDING ensures that no two same-width envelopes can ever appear as an increasing pair in the height sequence (since their heights only decrease relative to each other), correctly preventing invalid same-width "nesting."

Reducing to LIS: after this sort, the maximum nesting chain length equals the Longest Increasing Subsequence of the height sequence, solvable via the patience-sorting technique: maintain a list of the smallest tail height for each achievable subsequence length, using binary search to place each new height.

The core idea: a careful sort transforms a 2D nesting problem into the classical 1D Longest Increasing Subsequence problem, solvable in O(n log n).

Sort by width ascending, ties by height descending. Compute the Longest Increasing Subsequence of the resulting height sequence using binary search on a "tails" array: for each height, find its insertion point among the tails, extending or replacing accordingly.

blocks.caption: After the careful sort, the answer is the Longest Increasing Subsequence length of the heights

blocks.text: Sorting by width ascending guarantees any subsequence of the sorted order has non-decreasing widths; breaking ties by height descending guarantees that same-width envelopes can never both appear in an increasing height run (since their relative heights only decrease). This means a strictly increasing subsequence of the height sequence exactly corresponds to a valid nesting chain (strictly increasing in BOTH width and height). The patience-sorting LIS technique correctly computes the length of the longest such subsequence in O(n log n), by maintaining the smallest possible tail height for each achievable chain length.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), for the sort plus the binary-search-based LIS computation.
Space: O(n) for the tails array.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "nest objects requiring strict improvement in BOTH dimensions", think: sort by one dimension (careful tie-break), then Longest Increasing Subsequence on the other.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The O(n squared) direct DP approach is too slow for large inputs; the sort-plus-LIS approach runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space, the standard expected solution.

items: Pattern: reduce a 2D nesting/dominance problem to the classical 1D Longest Increasing Subsequence problem via a careful sort.
Core Idea: sort by width ascending (ties by height descending), then compute the Longest Increasing Subsequence of heights using binary search.
Time: O(n squared) for the direct pairwise DP, O(n log n) for the sort-plus-LIS approach.
Most Important Observation: the descending tie-break on height is what makes the width-then-height reduction to 1D LIS actually correct.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, elegant reduction problem connecting 2D dominance to 1D LIS.
One line memory trick: sort width up, height down on ties, then find the Longest Increasing Subsequence of heights.
